newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: CZECH C.BANK SPLITS AGROBANKA ASSETS.
newsitem.headline: CZECH C.BANK SPLITS AGROBANKA ASSETS.

text.p: The Czech central bank on Friday said it had split the assets of troubled bank Agrobanka a.s. into two parts -- questionable assets and sound assets -- allowing for the sound assets to be sold off in a tender.

A joint statement with Agrobanka and the central bank's administrators -- Agrobanka was placed under temporary forced administration by the central bank last September after it experienced liquidity problems -- did not say what the assets of each part totalled.
"The recmommended option fully meets the objectives of the administration," the statement quoted central bank administrator Jiri Klumpar as saying.

"It allows, contrary to a capital reduction, existing shareholders the opportunity to retain an interest in those assets agfainst which substantial provisions are required by the auditors. These provisions give rise to a large deficit in the net assets of the bank at this time."

Agrobanka is the fifth largest Czech bank, and the largest fully private financial institution in the country in terms of assets. It had a 372 million crown net profit in 1995, after 171 million in 1994.
It was put under a forced administration of the central bank in September after a liquidity crisis threatened the bank.
The statement added that preparations for the internal reorganisation of the bank will start immediately, allowing for the rapid sale of the new division.

"The creation of a strong separate division of Agrobanka is likely to attract considerable interest from leading international commercial banks committed to the development of the Czech banking system," said John Sleeman, director of investment bank HSBC, which is arranging the tender.
Agrobanka has said that U.S. General Electric Capital Corp, and Austria's Raiffeisen bank, are among five bidders seeking a stake in the Prague-based bank through the tender.
Agrobanka experienced liquidity problems when it was connected to the failure of a smaller Plzen-based bank, Kreditni Banka a.s..
The failure of Kreditni, which investigators said was caused by dubious debt-swap deals linked to Motoinvest, a secretive investment firm, in turn caused a crisis in confidence in Agrobanka.

Agrobanka was the 12th and so far the largest Czech bank to have been subjected to central bank intervention since post-Communist liberalisation of the sector created dozens of new banks in the early 1990s.

After the wave of collapses, the central bank drew up a plan under which an arm of the state-held Konsolidacni Banka would buy off doubtful assets from small banks at a nominal price for a certain period of time, but the banks would have to adhere to strict rules and close central bank supervision.
